name: Fortissimo-Surge
geological_features: Rocky seamounts that nearly breach the surface during low tides
Submarine canyon systems carved by powerful deep currents
Mineral-rich black smoker fields along spreading ridges
specific_features: The Thunderwave — periodic rogue waves over 200 meters tall generated by submarine landslides
Sonic shrimp colonies whose collective snapping creates underwater shockwaves detectable from orbit
resources: Polymetallic sulfide deposits at hydrothermal vents
Piezoelectric organisms that generate harvestable electricity
Dense protein-rich biomass in mid-ocean layers
description: Fortissimo-Surge is a loud world. Its ocean is dominated by powerful currents, submarine landslides, and an extraordinary density of sonic fauna whose collective noise output makes it one of the most acoustically intense environments ever recorded. The surface is constantly agitated, with whitecap waves and frequent rogue waves generated by the unstable submarine geology.

The dense atmosphere amplifies and transmits the ocean's noise, creating a wall of sound that greets any approaching vessel. Submersible crews report that the deep ocean is even louder, with the combined snapping of trillions of sonic shrimp-analogues producing a continuous roar punctuated by the groaning of shifting seamounts. Communication equipment must be specially shielded against the acoustic interference.

The sonic shrimp colonies are the planet's keystone species, and their numbers have been declining for decades. The cause appears to be a parasitic organism that attacks their sound-producing organs, silencing them and disrupting the acoustic ecology that the entire food web depends upon. As the shrimp fall silent, their predators starve and the cascading effects ripple through every level of the ecosystem.

Marine biologists are racing to understand and counter the parasite before the acoustic ecosystem collapses entirely. The irony is that the planet's noise — which makes research operations difficult and dangerous — may be the very thing that needs saving. Several pharmaceutical companies have offered to fund research in exchange for exclusive rights to the shrimp's piezoelectric biology, raising uncomfortable questions about who truly benefits from conservation.
